Improved anaerobic digestion performance of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus by
diﬀerent pretreatment methods and preliminary economic analysis
Shan-Fei Fua,b, Kai-Qiang Chena, Rong Zhua,b, Wen-Xin Suna, Hua Zoua,b,⁎, Rong-Bo Guoc,⁎
a School of Environment and Civil Engineering, Jiangnan University, Wuxi, Jiangsu Province 214122, PR China
b Jiangsu Key Laboratory of Anaerobic Biotechnology, Jiangnan University, Wuxi, Jiangsu Province 214122, PR China
c Shandong Industrial Engineering Laboratory of Biogas Production & Utilization, Qingdao Institute of Bioenergy and Bioprocess Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences,
Qingdao, Shandong Province 266101, PR China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Anaerobic digestion
Pretreatment
Methane yield
Structure changes
Preliminary economic analysis
A B S T R A C T
During the anaerobic digestion (AD) of cellulosic substrate, an economical and environmental friendly pre-
treatment method should be selected to improve the AD performance. In this study, ﬁve pretreatment methods
include four traditional pretreatment methods (alkali hydrogen peroxide pretreatment, NaOH pretreatment, HCl
pretreatment and hot water pretreatment) and one new developed pretreatment (microaerobic pretreatment)
method were selected to study the eﬀects of pretreatment on the AD of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus. In addition, pre-
liminary economic analysis of diﬀerent pretreatment methods was also conducted. Results showed pretreatment
could signiﬁcantly improve the AD performance of Miscanthus. After alkali hydrogen peroxide pretreatment,
microaerobic pretreatment, NaOH pretreatment, HCl pretreatment and hot water pretreatment the methane
yields of Miscanthus were 41.1%, 25.5%, 18.7%, 15.7% and 10.2% higher than that of untreated sample. Though
all these ﬁve pretreatment methods could improve the methane yield signiﬁcantly, their action sites were dif-
ferent. H2O2 pretreatment and NaOH pretreatment were eﬃcient in removal lignin from Miscanthus ﬂoridulus.
Hemicellulose structure was also partly destroyed during H2O2 pretreatment and NaOH pretreatment. HCl
pretreatment was eﬃcient in destruction of hemicelluloses structure and partly destroyed the cellulose structure.
Microaerobic pretreatment and hot water pretreatment were mainly acted in partly destruction of hemicelluloses
and cellulose components. Preliminary economic analysis showed compared with un-pretreated group only
microaerobic pretreatment was economically feasible. In addition, compared with other pretreatment methods,
microaerobic pretreatment just needs limited amount of oxygen, which is more environmental friendly.
1. Introduction
Due to the energy shortage and environmental pollution, bio-me-
thane production from organic waste through AD method has attracted
increasing attention [1–3]. Miscanthus is a tall perennial grass with high
water and nitrogen use eﬃciency [4–6]. In addition, biomass yields of
Miscanthus is much higher, Miscanthus can also well adapt to diﬀerent
climate and soil conditions [4,6]. These all make Miscanthus to be a
potential substrate for biogas production. Miscanthus is a lignin rich
substrate, and the hemicellulose in Miscanthus was encircled by com-
pact lignin structure. Therefore, the AD of Miscanthus is always in-
eﬃcient [7]. During the AD of Miscanthus, appropriate pretreatment is
essential to destroy the compact structure and improve the AD eﬃ-
ciency [5].
Using pretreatment methods to improve the AD performance of
cellulosic
substrate
has
been
widely
studied
[8–10].
Alkali
pretreatment, acid pretreatment, alkali hydrogen peroxide pretreat-
ment, hot water pretreatment and biological pretreatment are among
the most studied pretreatment method. Alkali pretreatment mainly acts
in removal/destruction the lignin structure or dissolution the hemi-
celluloses structure [11,12]. The most common alkalis during alkali
pretreatment were NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)2 and NH3·H2O, among which
NaOH was the most studied and was thought to be the most eﬃcient
[13]. Acid pretreatment has little impact on the lignin structure of
cellulosic substrate, which mainly acted with the cellulose structure.
After acid pretreatment, the cellulose structure was partly destroyed or
became more sensitive to relative enzyme [13]. Both inorganic (e.g.
H2SO4, HCl, HNO3, H3PO4) and organic acids (e.g. acetic acid, maleic
acid) were widely used during acid pretreatment. Alkali hydrogen
peroxide pretreatment could destroy the lignin structure of cellulosic
substrate by the strong oxidizing property of hydrogen peroxide. During
hydrogen peroxide pretreatment, the pH of pretreatment system was a

critical factor, studies showed at the pH of 11.8 the deligniﬁcation was
best [14]. During hot water pretreatment, water could penetrate into
the cellulosic structure and destroy hemiacetal linkages of hemi-
celluloses, which could liberate O-acetyl and other acid moieties. The
released acids in turn could accelerate the removal of oligosaccharides
from hemicellulose [15]. Biological pretreatment mainly achieved by
addition of bacterial or fungal strain or a consortium of bacteria and/or
fungi, with high capacity of degrading cellulose/hemicelluloses/lignin
[16]. An advanced biological pretreatment using fungal solid state
fermentation was reported by Yahmed et al., which enhanced biogas
production of 21% [17]. There were no toxic compound productions
and additional chemical needed during biological pretreatment and the
biological pretreatment could conduct at mild condition. Therefore,
biological pretreatment received increasing attentions.
Capital cost and environmental implication of the applied pre-
treatment method are also a critical aspect except the improved AD
eﬃciency.
During
the
application
of
conventional
pretreatments
method, additional energy or chemicals are required, which may lead
to increased capital cost. The study of Passos et al. [18] showed al-
though thermochemical pretreatment increased the methane potential
of dairy cow manure, AD without pretreatment was more economical.
In addition, inhibitory and biologically non-degradable compounds
may also generate during these traditional pretreatment method. Mi-
chalsk and Ledakowicz [19] found although H2O2 decomposition could
degrade energy plant signiﬁcantly, however, the biogas production was
strongly inhibited by byproducts of the pretreatment process. These all
hold up the engineering application of these pretreatment methods.
Therefore, an economic feasible and environmental friendly pretreat-
ment method still needed to develop. Recently studies showed a novel
biological pretreatment-microaerobic pretreatment is also an alter-
native pretreatment method both for solid substrate (e.g. cellulosic
substrate) and liquid substrate (e.g. food waste and brown water)
during the AD process [20–22]. During microaerobic pretreatment,
aerobic/facultative microorganisms could be enriched and keep high
activity, which would in turn produce more extracellular enzymes (e.g.
cellulase). The produced extracellular enzymes could react with sub-
strate and therefore improve the hydrolysis rate. As a novel pretreat-
ment, microaerobic pretreatment has several advantages e.g. no addi-
tional chemicals need, moderate environmental condition. Therefore,
further study of microaerobic pretreatment is needed.
In the present study, in order to select an economically feasible and
environmental friendly pretreatment method for the AD of Miscanthus,
the technical and preliminary economical evaluation of ﬁve pretreat-
ment methods include four traditional pretreatment methods (alkali
hydrogen peroxide pretreatment, NaOH pretreatment, HCl pretreat-
ment and hot water pretreatment) and one new developed pretreatment
(microaerobic pretreatment) method were conducted. The eﬀects of
diﬀerent pretreatment on the structure, methane yield and fermenta-
tion kinetics of Miscanthus were studied and compared.
2. Methods and materials
2.1. Substrate and inoculum during AD
Miscanthus ﬂoridulus used in this study was collected from HuNan
province (China), before further use, Miscanthus ﬂoridulus was air dried
to a TS (Total Solid) of 83.45 ± 0.6% with VS of 93.70 ± 0.64%. The
hemicelluloses, cellulose and lignin content of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus
were 23.78 ± 0.19%, 30.15 ± 0.05% and 25.91 ± 0.09% (based on
TS), respectively.
Inoculum used in this study was biogas slurry, collected from a
500 m3 size of biogas plant (Qingdao, Shandong province, China). The
biogas plant used corn straw as feedstock and running at 35 °C with
Hydraulic Retention Time (HRT) of 35d. The TS and VS of biogas slurry
were 6.72 ± 0.1% and 78.73 ± 0.1% (based on TS), respectively. The
collected biogas slurry was stored in a refrigerator at 4 °C, before AD,
the biogas slurry was pre-incubated at 37 °C for 3 days.
2.2. Pretreatment of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus
In this study, ﬁve pretreatment methods were selected: NaOH pre-
treatment, HCl pretreatment, hot water (low temperature) pretreat-
ment, alkali H2O2 pretreatment and thermophilic microaerobic pre-
treatment. During NaOH pretreatment, 6% NaOH solution was used,
the liquid to solid ratio was 10 ml/g and performed at 35 °C for 3 h [23].
During HCl pretreatment, the pH of pretreatment system was adjusted
to 1 with HCl, liquid to solid ratio was 10 ml/g and performed at 99 °C
for 30 min [24]. The hot water (low temperature) pretreatment was
performed at 95 °C for 10 h, the liquid to solid ratio was 10 ml/g
[25,26]. During alkali H2O2 pretreatment, 2% H2O2 solution was used,
the liquid to solid ratio was 10 ml/g and performed at 35 °C for 24 h,
before pretreatment the pH of this pretreatment system was adjusted to
11.8 with 2 M NaOH solution [27]. Microaerobic pretreatment was
conducted in 300 ml digester bottles, during which biogas slurry was
used as inoculum (the TS ratio of inoculum and substrate was 1:4) and
the oxygen load of microaerobic pretreatment was set as 5 ml/g VS (VS
of substrate). The oxygen needed was injected into the digester bottles
by syringe and then the digester bottles were placed in a shaking water
bath at 55 °C [22].
2.3. Batch AD of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus
Quadruplicate AD of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus was conducted in 300 ml
digester bottles with a working volume of 200 ml. After pretreatment,
pH of the system was adjusted to 7.2 with 2 M NaOH and 2 M HCl. After
that 40 ml biogas slurry was added, the working volume during AD was
adjusted to 200 ml with nutrient solution as Angelidaki et al. [28] de-
scribed. Batch AD of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus was conducted in shaking
water bath at 37 °C with 120 rpm.
2.4. The structure analysis of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus
In this study, the structure changes of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus were
analyzed by wide angle X-ray diﬀraction (XRD, Bruker D8 Advance)
and Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, S-4800 Hitachi). The crys-
tallinity index (CrI) of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus was calculated as following:
CrI = [(I002 −Im)/I002] × 100. Among which I002 is the intensity for
the crystalline portion at about 2θ = 22 and Im is the peak for the
amorphous portion at about 2θ = 16.2 [29].

ﬂoridulus, the Modiﬁed Gomperz equation as Zhang et al. [30] and Cai
et al. [31] described was used to ﬁt the methane production data. The
Modiﬁed Gomperz equation was written as following:

[18]. During the Preliminary economic analysis process, the AD system

3. Results and discussion
3.1. The structure changes of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus after diﬀerent
pretreatment methods
3.1.1. The eﬀect of pretreatment on the hemicelluloses, cellulose and lignin
contents of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus
Cellulosic substrates like Miscanthus ﬂoridulus are mainly composed
by hemicelluloses, cellulose and lignin, these three components hinge
with each other by non-covalent and covalent cross-linkage, which
makes the structure of cellulosic substrate stable [34,35]. Pretreatment
methods are widely used to improve the AD eﬃciency mainly by de-
struction the strong interlinkage among these three components,
breaking down lignin interference, reducing cellulose crystallinity or
increasing surface area [36,37]. The hemicelluloses, cellulose and
lignin contents of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus before and after pretreatment
were shown in Table 2. “Degradation rate” in Table 2 means the per-
cents of cellulose, hemicelluloses, lignin removed during pretreatment
process. It was calculated as following (taking cellulose as example):
Degradation rate = (initial percent of cellulose ∗initial TS of Miscanthus
– percent of cellulose after pretreatment ∗TS of Miscanthus after pre-
treatment)/initial percent of cellulose ∗initial TS of Miscanthus.
Pretreatment showed obvious impact on the hemicelluloses, cellu-
lose and lignin contents of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus. Among these 5 pre-
treatment methods, H2O2 pretreatment and NaOH pretreatment were
eﬃcient in removal lignin from Miscanthus ﬂoridulus. Also, the hemi-
cellulose structure was partly destroyed during H2O2 pretreatment and
NaOH pretreatment. HCl pretreatment was eﬃcient in destruction of
hemicelluloses structure and partly destroyed the hemicellulose struc-
ture. Microaerobic pretreatment and hot water pretreatment were
mainly acted in partly destruction of hemicelluloses and cellulose
components. However, the impact of hot water pretreatment on the
hemicelluloses and cellulose contents of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus was less,
which might due to the running condition of hot water pretreatment
was mild (95 °C for 10 h) compared with typical hot water pretreatment
(usually at higher temperature e.g. 150 °C [38], 190 °C [39]). Results
obtained from this study were quite consistent with previous studies,
NaOH pretreatment mainly acted in lignin removal from cellulosic
substrate [12,40], H2O2 pretreatment acted eﬃciently in destruction of
lignin structure[27,41], HCl pretreatment and microaerobic pretreat-
ment mainly acted in destruction of hemicelluloses and cellulose
structure [22,42]. The destroyed Miscanthus ﬂoridulus after pretreat-
ment was more accessible for enzymes during the AD process (espe-
cially the hydrolysis process), which led to higher methane production
rate and ﬁnally led to increased methane yield (shown as Figs. S2, 3 and
Table 4).
3.1.2. The eﬀect of pretreatment on the crystallinity index of Miscanthus
ﬂoridulus
The crystallinity of the cellulosic substrate is broadly accepted to be
unfavorable for the enzyme access [43], which is an important factor
during the AD process. The crystallinity indexes of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus
before and after pretreatment were shown in Table 3 and Fig. 1. Dif-
ferent pretreatment methods showed unequal impacts to the crystal-
linity index of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus. After NaOH pretreatment and H2O2
pretreatment, the crystallinity index of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus increased.
Relatively, after hot water pretreatment, microaerobic pretreatment
and HCl pretreatment the crystallinity index of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus
decreased. Unequal impacts to the crystallinity index of diﬀerent pre-
treatment methods correspond with the mechanisms of these pretreat-
ment methods. Crystallinity index (CrI = [(I002 −Im)/I002] × 100) of
Miscanthus ﬂoridulus was aﬀected by both the contents of amorphous

Table 2, NaOH pretreatment and H2O2 pretreatment mainly acted in
lignin and hemicellulose removal or destruction of lignin structure from
cellulosic substrate, they had little eﬀect on crystalline cellulose
structure. The removal of amorphous structure (lignin or hemicellulose)
might be the reason for the increased crystallinity index after NaOH
pretreatment and H2O2 pretreatment. Hot water pretreatment, micro-

tion of cellulose structure. However, they had little eﬀect on amorphous
structure (e.g. lignin). Therefore, after hot water pretreatment, micro-
aerobic pretreatment and HCl pretreatment the crystallinity index of
Miscanthus ﬂoridulus all increased. The XRD analyses results were quite
consistent with the structure analyses results (shown in Table 2). The
partly destructions of compact structure during pretreatment process
were the basis for the improved AD performance of pretreated Mis-
canthus ﬂoridulus.
3.1.3. The eﬀect of pretreatment on the microstructure of Miscanthus
ﬂoridulus
Pretreatment was also widely used to increase the surface area of
cellulosic substrate, therefore improved the enzyme access and ﬁnally
improved the AD eﬃciency. In this study, the microstructures of pre-
treated and untreated Miscanthus ﬂoridulus were observed by SEM, the
SEM images were shown in Fig. 2. Before pretreatment, Miscanthus
ﬂoridulus was intact with smooth and compact surface, there were even
no pores on the surface of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus. After pretreatment, the
intact surface of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus was destroyed. Especially after
NaOH pretreatment and H2O2 pretreatment, many pores appeared on
the surface, which might cause by the removal of lignin during these
two pretreatment. The destroyed intact surface and appeared pores
could greatly enhance the enzyme access. Therefore the AD of pre-
treated Miscanthus ﬂoridulus was more eﬃcient, which also led to
higher methane yield from pretreated Miscanthus ﬂoridulus.
3.2. Methane production from Miscanthus ﬂoridulus
The cumulative methane yields during AD of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus
were shown in Fig. 3. Results showed pretreatment before AD led to
improved methane yield from Miscanthus ﬂoridulus. Among these ﬁve
pretreatment methods, methane yield of H2O2 pretreated Miscanthus
ﬂoridulus was highest, which was 334 ml/g VSsubstrate and 41.1% higher
than that of control (without pretreatment). Methane yield from NaOH
pretreated Miscanthus ﬂoridulus was in second place, which was
297.1 ml/g VSsubstrate and 25.5% higher than that of control. Methane
yields from microaerobic pretreated, HCl pretreated and hot water
pretreated Miscanthus ﬂoridulus were 281, 273.8 and 260.9 ml/g
VSsubstrate respectively, which were 18.7%, 15.7% and 10.2% higher
than that of control, respectively. Statistical analysis of the methane
yields from Miscanthus ﬂoridulus with diﬀerent pretreatments were
conducted using the software of Microsoft Oﬃce Excel 2007. Pairwise
comparisons of methane yields from Miscanthus ﬂoridulus with diﬀerent
pretreatments were carried out by z-test and the signiﬁcant level was
set as 0.05. Statistical analysis results showed methane yields from
pretreated Miscanthus ﬂoridulus (except hot water pretreated Miscanthus
ﬂoridulus, p = .09 > .05) were statistically signiﬁcant higher than that
of control (p < .05). However, methane yields between diﬀerent pre-
treatments had no statistically signiﬁcant diﬀerences (except H2O2
pretreatment and hot water pretreatment, p = .02 < .05). Among
these 5 pretreatment methods, H2O2 pretreatment obtained highest
cumulative methane yield. However, H2O2 pretreatment needs con-
siderable amounts of H2O2 and NaOH to maintain the pretreatment
condition. Alkali pretreatment and acid pretreatment also need large
amount of alkali or acid to proceed the pretreatment process. In addi-
tion, after alkali pretreatment, acid pretreatment and H2O2 pretreat-
ment, additional chemicals (acid or alkali) also need to adjust the pH of
the AD system. In comparison, microaerobic pretreatment also led to
higher methane yield from Miscanthus ﬂoridulus (18.7% higher than
that of control) and microaerobic pretreatment just needs limited
oxygen or air, which is more economical and environmental friendly.
Modiﬁed Gomperz equation ﬁtting results were shown in Table 3. All
the R2 were greater than 98.6%, which means the methane data could
be well explained by the ﬁtting results. Among these ﬁve pretreatment
methods, maximum daily methane yield of 18.3 ml/g VSsubstrate per day

3.3. The SCOD concentration and pH value variations during the AD of
Miscanthus ﬂoridulus
The SCOD concentration and pH value variations during the AD of
Miscanthus ﬂoridulus were shown in Fig. 4. The parameter of SCOD
represents the solution extent of substrate, which is the dynamic
equilibrium between the solution of substrate into SCOD and the con-
sumption of SCOD to produce methane/carbon dioxide. During the
initial stage of AD, the SCOD concentration of the fermentation system

The pH value is also a crucial parameter of AD. The optimal pH
range for AD is 6.8–7.2 [47], a lower or higher pH value may lead
inhibition to AD system. The pH values of NaOH pretreated, hot water
pretreated, thermophilic microaerobic pretreated and un-pretreated
groups were always among 6.8–7.2. Similarly, pairwise comparisons of
pH with diﬀerent pretreatments were carried out also by t-test at the
two-sided signiﬁcance level p = .05. Statistical analysis results showed
pH during the whole AD process had no signiﬁcant diﬀerences between
diﬀerent groups. However, pH of un-pretreated group during 3rd day to
9th day was signiﬁcant higher than those of HCl and H2O2 pretreated
groups. At the 6th day of AD, the pH value of HCl pretreated group
dropped to 6.5 and recovered to more than 6.6, rapidly. Between the
3rd to 9th days of AD, the pH value of H2O2 pretreated group was lower
than 6.6. During H2O2 pretreatment, the dense structure of substrate
was destroyed more radical (as shown in Table 1 and Fig. 2), which led
to higher hydrolysis rate in H2O2 pretreated group. These were also the
reason for the longer lag-phase time of H2O2 pretreated group and
lower biogas-production eﬃciency during this period (shown in Table 4
and Fig. S2).
3.4. Preliminary economic analysis of diﬀerent pretreatment methods
The Preliminary economic analysis results were shown in Table 5.
Due to the improved input caused by chemical/energy, the costs to
produce per cubic meter biomethane of these four traditional pre-
treatments (alkali hydrogen peroxide pretreatment, NaOH pretreat-
ment, HCl pretreatment and hot water pretreatment) were higher than
that of control. Similar results were also widely reported in other stu-
dies. Study carried out by Passos et al. [18], who made the experi-
mental and economic evaluation of thermochemical pretreatment
during the AD of dairy cow manure. Even the methane potential of
dairy cow manure could be signiﬁcantly improved after thermal-alkali
or thermal-acid pretreatment, the untreated group was more econom-
ically feasible. The economically feasible of pretreatment might be af-
fected by pretreatment types and conditions applied and improved
methane yield after pretreatment. As Ruﬃno Barbara et al. demon-
strated if NaOH pretreatment was carried out at dose of 0.08 g NaOH/g
TS, 60% increase of the methane yield could oﬀset the cost of chemicals
[48]. In order to improve the economical performance of chemical/
thermal pretreatment methods, researches of chemical (e.g. NaOH,
HCl) reuse technologies and energy recovery technologies during the
pretreatment process are urgently needed. Among these ﬁve pretreat-
ment methods, only the microaerobic pretreatment group obtained a
lower cost than un-pretreated group to produce per cubic meter bio-
methane. Meanwhile, during the microaerobic pretreatment, there
were no additional chemicals needs. Therefore, compared with other
pretreatment methods, microaerobic pretreatment is more economical
and environmental friendly.
4. Conclusions
The technical and preliminary economical analysis of ﬁve pre-
treatment methods was conducted in the present study. The AD eﬃ-
ciency of Miscanthus could be signiﬁcantly improved by the pretreat-
ment process. Diﬀerent pretreatments have unequal eﬀects on the
structure of Miscanthus. Among the ﬁve pretreatment methods, alkali
hydrogen peroxide pretreatment was most eﬃcient in improving the
methane yield, however the start-up performance of microaerobic
pretreated Miscanthus was best. Preliminary economical analysis
showed only microaerobic pretreatment among these ﬁve pretreatment
methods was economically feasible. In order to improve the economical
performance of chemical/thermal pretreatment methods, researches of
chemical (e.g. NaOH, HCl) reuse technologies/energy recovery tech-
nologies during the pretreatment process are urgently needed. Based on
the results obtained in current study, microaerobic pretreatment is an
attractive pretreatment method which is both economically feasible and
environmental friendly during the AD of cellulosic substrate (e.g.
Miscanthus).
